readings.c1s1:
{{smaller block|<poem>And when thow shalt grow ''twychild'', she will bee
Carefull and kinde (religiously) to thee.</poem>
{{right|''Davies'', Scourge of Folly, p. 218. (''Halliwell.'')}}}}

'''twick†''' (twik), ''v.'' [< ME. ''twikken'', ''twykken''; the unassibilated form of ''twitch''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''tweak''<sup>1</sup> and ''twig''<sup>2</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To tweak; twitch.
{{smaller block|<poem>Voide leves puld to be . . .
With fyngers lightly ''twyk'' hem from the tree.</poem>
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 150.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To jerk or haul, as at a rope.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Quartus Tortor.'' Som can ''twyk'', who so it is,
Sekes easse on som kyn syde.
''Primus Tortor.'' It is better, as I hope,
Oone by his self to draw this rope.</poem>
{{right|''Towneley Mysteries'', p. 220.}}}}

'''twick''' (twik), ''n.'' [< ''twick'', ''v.'' Cf. ''twitch''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', and ''twig''<sup>2</sup>.] A twitch; a tweak; a sudden jerk. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''twick-bine''' (twik′bīn), ''n.'' The rowan, ''Pyrus Aucuparia. Britten and Holland.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''twiddle''' (twid′l), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''twiddled'', ppr. ''twiddling''. [Formerly also ''twidle'', also ''tweedle''; origin obscure. Cf. ''quiddle''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To twirl idly; hence, to fiddle or play with.
{{smaller block|“May I be allowed to walk with you as far as your house?” says Philip, ''twiddling'' a little locket which he wore at his watch-chain. {{right|''Thackeray'', Philip, xiv.}}

Straw-colored crickets that sit and ''twiddle'' their long antennæ at you as if they never intended moving again.
{{right|''P. Robinson'', Under the Sun, p. 72.}}

Then he sat silent for a moment, staring into the fire and ''twiddling'' his thumbs, unconscious of what he was doing. {{right|''Mrs. Oliphant'', Poor Gentleman, ix.}}}}

'''2.''' To move or propel by repeated light touches.
readings.c1s2:
¶
{{smaller block|With my fingers upon the stupe, I pressed close upon it, and ''twidled'' it in, first one side, then the other.
{{right|''Wiseman'', Surgery.}}}}

'''To twiddle one’s fingers''', to do nothing; be idle. [Colloq.]

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To twirl; revolve.

{{smaller block|She rose, . . . made a majestic courtesy, during which all the bugles in her awful head-dress began to ''twiddle'' and quiver.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Book of Snobs, xxiv.}}}}

'''2.''' To play or trifle with something, as by touching or handling; toy.

{{smaller block|Marm, I seed him a ''twiddling'' with your gown. He done it for a lark arter the fair, and ought to stand something. ''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, I. 481.}}

'''3.''' To be busy about trifles; quiddle. [Prov. Eng.]

'''twiddle''' (twid′l), ''n.'' [< ''twiddle'', ''v.''] '''1.''' A slight twirl with the fingers.—'''2.''' A pimple. [Prov. Eng.]

'''twiddler''' (twid′lėr), ''n.'' [< ''twiddle'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who or that which twiddles.

{{smaller block|“Give you fair warning—look out, you know—that’s all,” said the mustachio-''twiddler.''
{{right|''Thackeray'', Vanity Fair, xiv.}}}}

'''twiddling-line''' (twid′ling-līn), ''n.'' '''1†.''' A small rope securing a ship’s steering-wheel when not in use.—'''2.''' A string fastened to one of the gimbals of a compass, and having its end hanging out of the binnacle so that the helmsman may by pulling it cause the compass-card to play freely.

'''twidle†''', ''v.'' See ''twiddle''.

'''twie†''' (twī), ''adv.'' [ME., also ''twye'', < AS. ''twiwa'', twice, < ''twi-'', ''twa'', two: see ''twi-'' and ''two''. Hence ''twies'', now ''twice''. Cf. ''thrie''<sup>2</sup>.] Two times; twice.
readings.c1s3:
{{smaller block|<poem>Ihc oȝte deie ''tuye'' with riȝte,
O [one] deth for the, on other for me.</poem>
{{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 70.}}}}

'''twier''' (twī′ėr), ''n.'' Same as ''twyer.''

'''twies†''', ''adv.'' An old spelling of ''twice.''

'''twifaced†''' (twī′fāst), ''a.'' [Also ''twyfaced''; < ''twi-'' + ''faced.''] Having two faces; hence, deceitful.
{{smaller block|And ''twy-fac’d'' fraud and beetle-brow’d distrust.
{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, v. 14.}}}}

'''twifallow†''' (twī′fal″ō), ''v. t.'' [Also ''twyfallow''; < ''twi-'' + ''fallow''<sup>2</sup>.] To plow a second time, as fallow land, to prepare it for seed.
{{smaller block|<poem>In May, at the furthest, ''twifallow'' thy land,
Much drought may else after cause plough for to stand.</poem>
{{right|''Tusser'', May’s Husbandry.}}
For my owne part, I was never so good a husband to take any delight to heare one of my ploughmen tell how an acre of wheat must be fallowed and ''twyfallowed.''
{{right|''Sir J. Harington'', Apol. of Poetry.}}}}

'''twifallow†''' (twī′fal″ō), ''n.'' [< ''twifallow, v.''] The process of twifallowing land.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Twifallow'' once ended, get tumbrell and man,
And compass that fallow, as soon as ye can.</poem>
{{right|''Tusser'', May’s Husbandry.}}}}

'''twifoil''' (twī′foil), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''twyfoil''; < ''twi-'' + ''foil''<sup>1</sup>.] In ''her.'', same as ''dufoil.''

'''twifold''' (twī′fōld), ''a.'' [Formerly also ''twyfold''; < ME. ''twifold'', ''twifald'', < AS. ''twifeald'' = OFries. ''twifald'' = OHG. ''zwifalt'', MHG. ''zwivalt'' (G. ''zwiefältig'') = Icel. ''tvīfaldr'', twofold; as ''twi-'' + ''-fold.'' Cf. ''twofold.''] Twofold. [Archaic.]

''twigges'', ''twygges''), with shortened vowel, earlier ''twīg'', ''twī'' (pl. ''twīges''), with long vowel, < AS. ''twīg'' (pl. ''twīgu'') = D. ''twijg'' = LG. ''twich'' = OHG. ''zwīg'', ''zwī'', MHG. ''zwīc'' (''zwīg-''), ''zwī'', G. ''zweig'', a twig; perhaps, with a formative ''-g'', orig. ''-j'', < ''twi-'', etc., two, with ref. to a forked twig; cf. ''twissel'', a forked twig, from the same source.] '''1.''' A small shoot of a tree or other plant; a small branch; a spray. {{smaller block|Take ferules eke, or saly ''twygges'' take Ye may. {{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 38.}} We liken a young childe to a greene ''twigge'', which ye may easilie bende euery way ye list. {{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 205.}} Who set the ''Twigs'' shall he remember That is in Haste to sell the Timber? {{right|''Prior'', Alma, iii.}}}} '''2.''' A divining-rod. {{smaller block|The latest revival among old beliefs is that in the divining-rod. “Our liberal shepherds give it a shorter name,” and so do our conservative peasants, calling the “rod of Jacob” the ''twig''. {{right|''Cornhill Mag.'', XLVII. 83.}}}} '''3.''' In ''ceram.'', a thin strip of prepared clay used in modeling a pottery vessel, especially in the imitation basketwork common in Leeds pottery.—'''To hop the twig.''' {{smaller|See ''hop''1.}}—'''To work the twig,''' {{smaller|to use the divining-rod. ''Cornhill Mag.'', XLVII. 83.}} '''twig'''1 (twig), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''twigged'', ppr. ''twigging''. [< ''twig''1, ''n.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To switch; beat. ''Halliwell.'' '''II.''' ''intrans.'' To be vigorous or active; be energetic. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.] Ewes yearly by twinning rich masters do make; The lamb of such twinners for breeders go take: For twinlings be twiggers, increase for to bring, Though some for their ''twigging'' peccavi may sing. {{smaller block|{{right|''Tusser'', January’s Husbandry.}}}} '''twig'''2 (twig), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''twigged'', ppr. ''twigging''. [A var. of ''twick'', unassibilated form of ''twitch'': see ''twick'', ''twitch''1, and cf. ''tweak''1.] To twitch; jerk. [Scotch.] {{smaller block|Not one kynge hath bene in Englande sens the conquest but they haue ''twygged'' hym one way or other, and had theyr false flynges at him. {{right|''Bp. Bale'', Apology, fol. 142.}} Let rantin billies ''twig'' the string, An’ for anither mutchkin ring. {{right|''Morison'', Poems, p. 78. (''Jamieson.'')}}}} '''twig'''2 (twig), ''n.'' [< ''twig''2, ''v.'' Cf. ''twick'', ''tweak''1, ''n.''] A twitch; a jerk; a quick, sudden pull. ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.] '''twig'''3 (twig), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''twigged'', ppr. ''twigging''. [Prob. < Ir. ''tuigim'', I understand, discern, = Gael. ''tuig'', understand.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To notice; observe narrowly; watch. {{smaller block|''Mug.'' Gentlemen of the Corporation of Garratt—— ''Heel-Tap.'' Now, ''twig'' him; now, mind him; mark how he hawls his muscles about. {{right|''Foote'', Mayor of Garratt, ii. 2.}} The word seems to have got into English through the ugliest kind of jargon, as in the choice morsel of thieves’ cant “''twig'' the cull, he ’s peery”: “observe the fellow, he is watching.” {{right|''Macmillan’s Mag.'' (''Imp. Dict.'')}}}} '''2.''' To comprehend; understand; perceive; discover. {{smaller block|From the sudden erubescence of his pallid, ill-fed cheek, . . . I ''twigged'' at once that he didn’t himself know what it meant. {{right|''Dr. J. Brown'', Spare Hours, 1st ser., p. 306.}}}} {{smaller block|What is that first instantaneous glimpse of some one’s meaning which we have when in vulgar phrase we say we ''twig'' it? {{right|''W. James'', Prin. of Psychology, I. 253.}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' To understand; see; “catch on.” {{smaller block|Don’t you ''twig?'' {{right|''T. Hook'', Gilbert Gurney, III. ii.}} “I ''twig'',” said Mick. {{right|''Disraeli'', Sybil, v. 10.}}}} [Slang in all uses.] '''twig-blight''' (twig′blīt), ''n.'' See ''pear-blight'', under ''blight.'' Compare ''twig''1, ''v. i.'' {{smaller block|Twinlings be ''twiggers'', increase for to bring. {{right|''Tusser'', January’s Husbandry.}}}} '''2†.''' A wanton person of either sex. {{smaller block|Now, Benedicite, her mother said; And hast thou beene already such a ''twigger?'' {{right|''Pasquil’s Night Cap'' (1612). (''Nares.'')}} The mother of her was a good ''twigger'' the whilst. {{right|''Middleton'', No Wit like a Woman’s, iv. 1.}}}} {{img float|file=century v08 p0355 c3f2.png|width=111px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Twig-girdler (''Oncideres cingulatus'').
''a'', beetle; ''b'', point of oviposition; ''c'', girdling of the twig; ''e'', egg.}}}} '''twig-girdler''' (twig′gėr″dlėr), ''n.'' A longicorn beetle, ''Oncideres cingulatus'', which girdles twigs of apple, oak, and other trees in the United States, producing a decaying condition of the wood fitting it as food for the larvæ. '''twiggy''' (twig′i), ''a.'' [< ''twig''1 + ''-y''1.] '''1.''' Consisting of or resembling twigs; made of twigs. {{smaller block|Small ''twiggie'' stalkes. {{right|''Gerarde'', Herball (1599), p. 804.}} Oziers . . . are of innumerable Kinds, . . . being so much smaller than the Sallows, . . . and requiring constant moisture. It likewise yields more limber and flexible twigs . . . for all wicker and ''twiggy'' works. {{right|''Evelyn'', Sylva, i. 20.}}}} '''2.''' Full of twigs. {{smaller block|They [the black withies] grow the slowest of all the ''twiggy'' trees. {{right|''Evelyn'', Sylva, i. 20.}}}} '''twight1†.''' An obsolete past participle of ''twitch''1. '''twight2†,''' ''v.'' An erroneous spelling of ''twit.'' ''Spenser'', F. Q., V. vi. 12. '''twig-insect''' (twig′in″sekt), ''n.'' Same as ''stick-bug'', 1. Also ''twig-bug.'' {{smaller block|“The so-called stick insects,” or “walking-twigs,” as they are often called — the Phasmidæ of the naturalist, “these ''twig insects.''” {{right|''R. Proctor'', Nature Studies.}}}} '''twigless''' (twig′les), ''a.'' [< ''twig''1 + ''-less.''] Lacking twigs. {{smaller block|Unbranching and ''twigless'' stems. {{right|''Nature'', XLII. 151.}}}} '''twig-pruner''' (twig′prö″nėr), ''n.'' A longicorn beetle of the genus ''Elaphidion.'' {{smaller|The larvæ of the parallel twig-pruner, ''E. parallelum'', live in the twigs of oak- and apple-trees and other forest- and fruit-trees in the northern United States, and pupate in their burrows. The beetles oviposit by preference in the cut ends of twigs, and the larvæ work into the live wood by boring down the center. See cut under ''Elaphidion'', and compare ''twig-borer.''}} '''twig-rush''' (twig′rush), ''n.'' A plant of the cyperaceous genus ''Cladium'', this name as well as the genus name referring to the repeatedly branching cyme of the original species, ''C. Mariscus.'' {{smaller|This is a tall perennial rush-like plant with long slender leaves toothed on the edges and the keel, found in bogs in most temperate and some tropical regions. It occurs in the western United States, and in the southern if the similar ''C. effusum'' (see ''saw-grass'') be included in it. ''C. mariscoides'' grows northward in North America. There are in all about 33 species.}}
